Mexico activity is collapsing (guided down 30–50%, then "around 60%"). A new chief financial officer, Anuj Dhruv, arrives on "day three."
- **Q2–Q3 2025:** The message becomes "we cannot control revenue, so we will control cash and cost." Headcount is cut by "over 2,000" and annualized personnel expense by "more than $145 million." The balance sheet is refinanced and de-levered; net leverage falls to roughly half a turn. Free cash flow is repeatedly the "North Star."
- **Q4 2025 (February 2026):** The first genuinely confident quarter in a year — sequential revenue growth, EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization) margin above 22%, free-cash-flow conversion of 76%, a 10% dividend increase, and a first mention of a possible Venezuela re-opening (once a $500M-revenue market).

**Rating: Stable (structurally strengthening franchise inside a cyclical revenue decline).**

- Q1 2026: confident on the long arc (offshore 2027), realistic on the near term (Iran).

**Reliability: High.** Weatherford lowered guidance first in the sector (early 2025), called Mexico's ~60% collapse quarters ahead, and then met or beat the lowered bar — Q3 2025 came "above the expectations that we outlined in July," and FY2025 free-cash-flow conversion (+576 bps) landed "well over our initial view" of +100–200 bps. - **"Less granular" guidance** is a quiet tell that visibility genuinely deteriorated in 2025.
- The **capital-allocation vocabulary migrated** from buybacks/dividends toward "capital-light," "working-capital efficiency," and "tax structure" — a shift from returning cash to re-engineering the cash engine (ERP, redomiciliation).
- The **redomiciliation target moved from Texas (Q1 2026 call) to Delaware (Q2 2026 release)** — the same initiative, restructured, now requiring a fresh shareholder vote on 3 September 2026 even though an earlier version already passed with ~89.78% support on 11 June 2026.
- New CFO Anuj Dhruv reframed the balance sheet as "a fortress" and set an *aspirational* free-cash-flow target "well above 50%," a subtle raising of the internal bar.

---

**Trajectory: STABLE.** This is a materially better-run, better-capitalized Weatherford than the one that emerged from bankruptcy — but it is a cyclical services business in a genuine downturn, and its revenue and earnings are falling now.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** the "deep value" label is a peak-earnings artifact. On normalized earnings power and on cash-flow multiples the stock is roughly *fairly valued* at ~$88, and it screens at a **premium** to oilfield-services peers on price-to-free-cash-flow (14.2x vs a typical 8–12x). The margin of safety only appears if the model uses 2023–2024 peak profits. Size for a fairly-valued quality cyclical, not for a mispriced bargain.

**Economic moat:** *narrow.* The durable edge is real but specific — technology and installed-base leadership in managed pressure drilling, artificial lift, and completions — sitting inside an otherwise price-competitive, capital-intensive service industry. Returns are decent but cyclical (return on invested capital ~13%, return on equity only ~3.9%). Margins and balance sheet are strengthening, so the moat is stable rather than eroding, but it is not wide.

**Secular threat:** *manageable.* The long-horizon energy-transition risk to oilfield services is real but not terminal for Weatherford, whose mix leans to production optimization, mature-field rejuvenation, gas, and offshore rather than to peak-demand-sensitive new-drilling. The cheapness is neither a clean fear-print nor a value trap — it is a fair price on a quality cyclical whose optical discount is a normalization illusion.

Free cash flow - the money left after running and re-equipping the business - was $466 million in 2025 at a 43.7% conversion of adjusted operating cash profit, an improvement of 576 basis points on 2024 against management's own promise of 100 to 200 points. In the first half of 2026 conversion ran near 49%, and the second quarter alone delivered $139 million at 62.3% conversion in a quarter disrupted by war, a Norwegian labour strike and deferred Mexican wells. Management has raised its full-year conversion target at four consecutive calls, from the low-40s in February to mid-to-high-40s in July, and the finance chief has said publicly that his private target sits above the stated 50% through-cycle goal. On a trailing twelve-month basis the company produced $525 million of free cash flow against a market value near $6.1 billion - a cash yield close to 8.6%, versus 6.2% at Halliburton, 5.9% at SLB and 5.5% at Baker Hughes. That is the cleanest single argument for owning this: it is the cheapest large oilfield-services name in the world on the metric that actually pays shareholders.

The second leg is the balance sheet, which is no longer a risk factor. Cash of $1.14 billion against $1.62 billion of total debt (including $176 million of leases) leaves net debt of $485 million and a net leverage ratio of 0.34 times - a level management describes as investment-grade equivalent. Total liquidity is $1.7 billion. The 2030 notes were refinanced out to 2033 in September 2025 at what management called the tightest spread to Treasuries an oilfield-services high-yield issuer had achieved, cutting roughly $35 million of annual interest. There is no maturity wall, no covenant pressure and no financing event that can force a bad decision. A cyclical with no solvency risk can wait out a cycle; that is what makes patience investable here rather than merely hopeful.

The third leg is cost and capital discipline that has been proven under fire. More than 2,000 positions and over $150 million of annualised cost came out in 2025, early and ahead of peers. Capital spending runs at 3.8% of revenue. Two Argentine businesses were sold because they were about to become capital-hungry. A Saudi lump-sum turnkey contract was allowed to lapse rather than be renewed at unacceptable pricing. The result is that adjusted operating margins held at roughly 20 to 22% through a 15% revenue decline from the 2024 peak - and the third quarter is guided up at least 100 basis points despite the Middle East conflict and the loss of that Saudi contract. Holding margin flat on a shrinking base is the single hardest thing to do in this industry, and this team has done it for eight quarters.

The fourth leg - the one not yet in the numbers - is the recovery. National oil companies are anchoring capital plans in security of supply; Brent crude sits near $100 a barrel; the deepwater cycle is visibly building, with second-quarter managed-pressure-drilling awards from Constellation, Ventura, Valaris, Noble and Esso Nigeria plus a five-year Chevron framework contract in Australia. Managed pressure drilling - drilling with precise control of downhole pressure - is Weatherford's genuine technology edge, and management sees roughly 30 drillships still to be equipped with it. Add Venezuela, a market that was once $500 million of annual revenue for this company and where management says it has been pleasantly surprised by the pace of reopening, with a tangible 2027 contribution expected. Add the Delaware redomestication approved on 3 September, worth $20-30 million of cash savings a year from 2027. Add NCS Multistage, closed 1 September, a capital-light completions business with at least $15 million of identified cost synergies within eighteen months and a global distribution network to scale into.

For this to work, three conditions must hold: the Middle East conflict must stop deteriorating so that the deferred activity actually returns; Mexican payments must keep arriving at the pace of the last three quarters; and 2027 must deliver the growth management says is coming. If all three hold, 2027 adjusted operating cash profit of $1.1 billion at better than 50% conversion plus the tax savings produces roughly $575 million of free cash flow, and a business converting cash at that rate with 0.3 times leverage does not stay at a 6.5 times multiple.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that Weatherford is a bad company. It is that you are being asked to pay roughly fair value for a business whose revenue has fallen for two straight years, whose recovery has been rescheduled six consecutive times, and whose upside depends entirely on one macro variable you cannot hedge inside the position.

Start with the trajectory. Revenue: $5.51 billion in 2024, $4.92 billion in 2025, a guided $4.54-4.80 billion in 2026. Adjusted operating cash profit is guided at $951 million to $1,046 million this year against roughly $1,066 million last year - so the 2026 guide is a third consecutive year of decline, not a trough with an upturn attached. Reported earnings per share went $6.75 (2024) to $5.93 (2025) to $5.07 on a trailing basis, and the second quarter of 2026 printed $0.55 against roughly $0.92 expected. Each individual decline has an explanation - Mexico, tariffs, the Iran conflict, a Norwegian strike, a 44% effective tax rate - and that is precisely the problem: for eight quarters there has always been an explanation.

Second, the recovery is a promise with a poor track record. In April 2025 the chief executive said headwinds would pass; in July 2025 he said they would persist for at least another twelve months; in October 2025 the hope moved to the second half of 2026; in February 2026 it became a tale of two halves; in April 2026 a new conflict arrived; in July 2026 it required, in his words, a recalibration on timing and pace. Management's own language is still hopeful rather than contracted - on Saudi recovery, on Mexican payments, on the conflict moderating, on industry pricing discipline. On 2027 the chief executive would say only that it should definitely be a year of growth while explicitly declining to size it. The number that matters does not exist until the February 2027 call.

Third, the conflict is not behind them. Management quantified the first-half profit impact at $30-50 million, then said on the July call that they expect it to increase over the year, and described a very unfortunate flare-up once again in the prior ten to twelve days, with continuing disruption in Bahrain, Qatar, Iraq and Kuwait. The cruel irony is structural: the $100 Brent price that is supposed to drive the recovery is itself partly a product of the same regional conflict that is suppressing Weatherford's activity in that region. High oil from a supply shock in the geography where you operate is a headwind, not a tailwind.

Fourth, the second half has identified revenue losses that are certain: the Saudi lump-sum contract concluded, and management said this will be further visible in the second half; the Oman integrated contract completed; and the replacement Marmul extension is smaller. Pricing pressure has been acknowledged on every call since mid-2025 and never quantified.

Fifth, concentration on three axes. One Mexican customer remains, by management's own words, the biggest driver of variability in the cash guidance - and the cash guidance is the entire bull case. The Middle East is simultaneously the growth engine and the war zone. And Russian revenue as a share of the enterprise has been rising, which management attributes to everything else shrinking - a sanctions escalation or forced exit is an unhedged tail that no analyst on any of the six calls has pressed.

Sixth, the people who know most are selling. On open-market transactions only, insiders bought 12,000 shares across two purchases and sold 178,370 shares across twelve. The flattering buy ratio in the screening data is inflated by share grants and should be disregarded.

Seventh, and decisively, the valuation is not distressed. At roughly 7.6 times enterprise value to trailing operating cash profit, Weatherford trades at only about a 7% discount to Halliburton's 8.1 times - and Halliburton is the correct comparison, because the 12 times multiples at SLB and Baker Hughes are inflated by large non-oilfield digital and industrial-technology businesses. The deep-value label in the screen comes from book-value and peak-earnings models: a stated 79% margin of safety and a $147.54 fair value both anchor on a 2024 earnings peak that will not be repeated soon, and one of the five internal models already reads fair to negative. Strip the peak-earnings artifact and the margin of safety is a few percent, not seventy.

What confirms the bear: a third-quarter print around 21 October that misses the $235-265 million operating-cash-profit guide or fails to deliver the promised 100 basis points of margin expansion; any Mexican payment interruption; a further Middle East escalation; or a 2027 guide in February that comes in flat rather than growing. There is no solvency risk here - just the risk of owning a fairly-priced cyclical for two years while the recovery is rescheduled a seventh time.
consensus_delta:
For a business the screen labels deeply undervalued, the right question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a company with stable earnings power. Our answer is that it is not - and that the apparent bargain is largely an artifact of how the value was measured.

Where the screen is wrong. The stated 79% margin of safety and the $147.54 fair value are anchored on 2024, which was the peak: revenue $5.51 billion, earnings per share $6.75. Applying peak multiples to a company guiding 2026 revenue of $4.54-4.80 billion and operating cash profit below 2025's level produces a number with no claim on reality. The internal models already disagree with each other by an enormous margin - a Graham-style reading says 71% undervalued while one of the other five reads negative - and wide model dispersion on a cyclical is nearly always a peak-earnings artifact rather than a hidden bargain. The screen's book-value-per-share growth of 36% a year over five years is likewise a post-bankruptcy accounting recovery, not compounding.

Where the street is wrong, and it cuts both ways. The consensus target of $135 is not a street-wide view: only one price target was published in the last quarter, five in the last year averaging $102.80, and the newest is 55 days old. The two recent marks bracket the argument - UBS upgraded to buy on 29 July with a $114 target when the stock was $83.58; Barclays carried $156 on 17 June at $97.85. Neither number has been refreshed for the September rate shock. A $135 consensus implies roughly 9.5 times enterprise value to operating cash profit, which is above Halliburton today, for a business with less scale and more geographic concentration. That target is stale, thin and too high.

Where we genuinely disagree with the market - and it is a smaller gap than it looks. The market prices Weatherford's cash conversion as though it were a cyclical accident. It is not: conversion has been raised at four consecutive calls, capital spending is structurally lower at 3.8% of revenue, working capital efficiency has improved two quarters running, the Delaware move adds $20-30 million of annual cash savings from 2027, and the refinancing cut roughly $35 million of interest. That is a durable step-change in free cash flow per dollar of revenue, and on free cash flow yield this is the cheapest large oilfield-services name in the world at 8.6% against Halliburton's 6.2%. But the market has already awarded most of that: closing even half the gap to Halliburton gets you to about $86, and the stock is $84.89. The disagreement is worth a few percent, not a re-rating.

The one genuinely underappreciated point is the earnings-per-share optics. Reported earnings fell 71% year on year in the second quarter, and the headline reads like a collapse. It is not: adjusted operating cash profit fell about 12%, and the gap is a $33 million tax charge on $75 million of pre-tax income - a 44% effective rate - against a tax benefit the prior quarter. This company misses consensus earnings estimates (four beats in seven quarters) because the tax and below-the-line lines are volatile, while it consistently hits the operating and cash figures it actually guides. Anyone screening on earnings-per-share momentum is reading the wrong line. That argues the business is better than the print - not that the stock is cheap.
forcing_function:
For a business priced on its cash generation rather than an event, the honest answer is that there is no single event that forces the re-rating - and pretending otherwise would be the error. What exists is a sequence of dated checkpoints, each of which either builds or breaks the case.

Around 21 October 2026 - third-quarter results. The hardest-edged date on the calendar and the first real test of the second-half recovery promise: $1.105-1.155 billion of revenue, $235-265 million of adjusted operating cash profit, margins up at least 100 basis points, more than $100 million of free cash flow, all while absorbing the concluded Saudi lump-sum contract, the completed Oman contract and the Norwegian strike. Clearing it would be the first hard evidence in six quarters that the inflection is real.

By 31 December 2026 - completion of the move of the corporate home to Delaware. Shareholders approved it on 3 September; Irish High Court approval is the remaining step and completion is expected by year-end. It delivers $20-30 million of annual cash savings from 2027 and simplifies the capital structure. Approved, largely priced, and worth about $3.40 a share in our base case.

February 2027 - full-year results and the 2027 guide. This is the real one. Management has explicitly deferred the size of 2027 growth to this date, saying only that 2027 should definitely be a year of growth. A guide that puts revenue back above $5 billion with operating cash profit above $1.1 billion would validate the whole thesis and would likely also carry the first quantified Venezuela contribution. A flat guide confirms the seventh reschedule.

Undated, but real: a free cash flow conversion print that sustainably clears 50%. The chief financial officer has said the stated 50% through-cycle target is his floor rather than his ambition. A company converting operating cash profit at better than half, with 0.3 times leverage and 4% capital intensity, does not durably trade at a discount to Halliburton.

What would make this actionable today is a price, not an event: the case becomes live in the $70-75 range, where the adverse scenario is largely in the price and the cash yield approaches 10%. That is the specific level we are waiting for.
valley_of_death:
There is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall. Net leverage is 0.34 times, cash is $1.14 billion, liquidity is $1.7 billion, the 2030 notes were pushed to 2033 in September 2025, and the business generated $139 million of free cash flow in its most disrupted quarter on record. Nothing here can force a bad decision. The risk in the next three to nine months is entirely to the share price and the narrative.

First, the Middle East. Management quantified the first-half profit impact at $30-50 million, then said in July that they expect it to increase over the year, and described a very unfortunate flare-up once again in the preceding ten to twelve days with disruption across Bahrain, Qatar, Iraq and Kuwait. The chief executive was explicit that the impact will unlikely go to zero until there is a firm and permanent resolution. Any further escalation lands directly on the region that was supposed to be the growth engine.

Second, the third-quarter print due around 21 October. The bar management set is specific: $1.105-1.155 billion of revenue, $235-265 million of adjusted operating cash profit, margins up at least 100 basis points, and more than $100 million of free cash flow. It has to be cleared while absorbing the concluded Saudi lump-sum contract, the completed Oman contract and a Norwegian labour strike that management said would remain a third-quarter headwind. A miss on the margin promise would be the first real break in an otherwise excellent guidance record.

Third, Mexico. Management calls collections from its largest customer there the biggest driver of variability in the cash guide - and cash is the entire investment case. Three consecutive quarters of sizeable payments is encouraging but it is not a contract, and the same customer deferred wells in the second quarter.

Fourth, and most immediately, the rate regime. The Federal Reserve raised rates on 16 September for the first time since July 2023, sixteen of eighteen participants pencil at least one further increase this year, and the ten-year Treasury closed at or above 5% on 16 and 18 September for the first time since 2007. Every cyclical with a back-loaded recovery gets marked down when the discount rate moves like that, and the oil-services complex did exactly that - down 7.4% in under three weeks. Another leg is entirely possible before any company-specific good news arrives.

Fifth, the February 2027 guidance call. Management has deferred the only number that matters - the size of 2027 growth - to that date. A flat guide would confirm a seventh reschedule.

Sixth, the unhedged tail nobody asks about: Russian revenue is a rising share of the enterprise. Management raised it themselves in July only to explain it away as a denominator effect. A sanctions escalation or forced exit is not in anyone's model.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling dynamic here, and it would be wrong to manufacture one. The dividend is not at risk - it was raised 10% in early 2026, costs roughly $80 million a year against $464-525 million of free cash flow, and both the chief executive and chief financial officer have called it sacrosanct. There is no pivot, no capital raise, no covenant, no index deletion in prospect and no yield-focused shareholder base to be flushed out; the stock yields roughly 1.2% and was never bought for income.

What the last three weeks did produce is mechanical, not fundamental, and it is worth naming precisely because it looks like distress and is not. The shares fell from $95.88 on 4 September to $82.03 by 18 September, and that session traded 3.0 million shares against a normal 700,000-900,000. The 18th was a triple-witching and index-rebalance date - option expiry colliding with index reconstitution - so the volume is rebalancing flow, not information. No company announcement was made between 3 September and today. The shares have already recovered 3.3% from that low, to $84.89.

The broader context matters more than the single session: the oil-services exchange-traded fund fell 7.4% over the identical window, so roughly two-thirds of Weatherford's decline is a sector-wide de-rating driven by the rate shock rather than anything specific to this company. The remaining third is idiosyncratic and unexplained by news - consistent with a small-capitalisation cyclical being sold by generalists reducing rate-sensitive exposure.

One genuinely negative positioning signal deserves weight: insiders are net sellers on open-market transactions, with 12,000 shares bought across two purchases against 178,370 shares sold across twelve. The favourable buy ratio in the screening data is inflated by share grants and should be disregarded. Management is buying back stock with company money - $16 million in the second quarter, over $370 million returned since inception - while selling their own. That is a common pattern and not damning, but it is not a vote of confidence either.

Conclusion: this is a de-rating, not a wash-out. There is no mechanical seller left to exhaust, which means there is no dislocation to exploit.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now - and this is a continuation of the prior committee's call, not a reversal.

The business case is not in dispute. Weatherford has made itself into a genuinely good oilfield-services company: net leverage of 0.34 times against 0.49 times a year ago, $1.7 billion of liquidity, free cash flow conversion raised at four consecutive calls, capital spending at 3.8% of revenue, more than $370 million returned to shareholders, a dividend raised 10%, and operating margins held near 20-22% through a 15% revenue decline from the 2024 peak - across a war, a labour strike, tariff dilution and a collapse in Mexico. Management called the downturn before its peers did, quantified an unquantifiable conflict impact and landed inside its own range, and has beaten every cash target it set. That earns a credibility score of 4 out of 5 and a genuine, if narrow, moat in managed pressure drilling and artificial lift.

The problem remains the price, and it has barely moved in our favour despite an 11.5% fall. That is the counterintuitive heart of this. The shares dropped from $95.88 on 4 September to $84.89 today - but roughly two-thirds of that is the oil-services complex de-rating 7.4% over the same window, and the reason it de-rated is that the discount rate moved: the Federal Reserve raised rates on 16 September for the first time since July 2023, sixteen of eighteen participants pencil another increase this year, and the ten-year Treasury closed at or above 5% for the first time since 2007. When the risk-free rate is 5%, a cyclical with a back-loaded recovery is worth less, and our own fair value fell roughly in step with the share price. Our base case is $88 against a $84.89 price - a margin of safety of a few percent, nowhere near the 20-30% this book requires before committing capital.

The market environment makes it worse, not better, in two specific ways. First, independence of drivers: the entire upside rests on global oil-directed capital spending, a single shared macro factor, in a market where that is exactly the concentration to avoid. Second, and more subtly, the $100 Brent price that is supposed to signal the recovery is partly a product of the same Middle East conflict that is suppressing Weatherford's activity in the Middle East. High oil from a supply shock in the geography where you operate is a headwind wearing a tailwind's clothes. What this thesis does not do is depend on rate cuts, which is to its credit.

On the catalyst we apply this book's neutrality rule strictly. Two dated events completed and are spent: the NCS Multistage acquisition closed 1 September, and shareholders approved the Delaware move on 3 September. Neither is penalised and neither is rewarded; both are simply credited in the base case, and together they are worth a few dollars a share. The forward driver - the second-half-2026-into-2027 recovery - is a soft catalyst with no fixed date, and it has now been rescheduled six consecutive quarters. We do not mark the name down for that; we mark it down for the absence of a discount.

The deep-value label does not survive contact with the live numbers. The 79% margin of safety and the $147.54 fair value are anchored on 2024 peak earnings that 2026 guidance will not come near; the internal models disagree violently, which on a cyclical is the signature of a peak-earnings artifact. Priced honestly against the only true peer - Halliburton, since SLB's and Baker Hughes's 12 times multiples are inflated by large non-oilfield businesses - Weatherford trades at 7.6 times operating cash profit against 8.1 times: a 7% discount. The one real relative-value argument is cash conversion, an 8.6% free cash flow yield against Halliburton's 6.2%, and closing even half that gap is worth about $86 a share. The market has already paid for most of it.

What we are waiting for, specifically: the case becomes live around $70-75, where the adverse scenario is largely in the price and the cash yield approaches 10%. Below $67 - our adverse case, which already assumes a persisting conflict and operating cash profit falling to $900 million - this would be a clear commitment, because the balance sheet means the downside is a long flat period rather than a permanent loss of capital. The other route in is evidence rather than price: a third-quarter print around 21 October that clears the margin promise, followed by a February 2027 guide with revenue back above $5 billion. That would convert a hope into a number, and we would revisit immediately.

Until one of those arrives, this is a good company at a fair price in a market that is repricing every fair-priced cyclical downward. Fair is not enough. Pass, and keep it close.

# Weatherford International (WFRD) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 2026-09-22 · **Price used:** $84.89 (Nasdaq, US dollars, live quote 2026-09-22; prior close $82.20)
**Transcripts reviewed:** Q1 2025 (2025-04-23) · Q2 2025 (2025-07-23) · Q3 2025 (2025-10-22) · Q4/FY 2025 (2026-02-04) · Q1 2026 (2026-04-22) · Q2 2026 (2026-07-22)

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Six consecutive calls tell one story told in two voices, and the split between them is the whole analytical problem with this company.

**The revenue voice has been in retreat for two years.** In April 2025 the chief executive, Girish Saligram, was the first in the sector to say the quiet part out loud: *"the market has taken a turn for the worse"*, Mexico was collapsing (revised from a 30–50% decline to roughly 60% inside one quarter), and tariffs *"will very likely cause demand destruction."* By July 2025 the language had hardened to *"we anticipate market headwinds will persist for at least another 12 months."* By February 2026 the frame had become a "tale of two halves" — first half soft, second half better. By April 2026 a new shock arrived that nobody had modelled: a conflict involving Iran that suspended projects across the Middle East, the one region that had been carrying the company. In July 2026 the recovery was pushed again: *"the ongoing geopolitical issues and the impact of demand destruction requires a recalibration on timing and pace."*

That is six straight quarters in which the promised inflection has been real in direction and wrong in timing. Revenue has gone $5.51B (2024) → $4.92B (2025) → a guided $4.54–4.80B for 2026. From the 2024 peak the top line will be down roughly 15%.

**The cash voice has done nothing but improve over the same period.** Free cash flow — the cash left after running and re-equipping the business — converted at 43.7% of adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA, a rough proxy for operating cash profit) in 2025, up 576 basis points on 2024 and far beyond the 100–200 point improvement management had promised entering the year. The 2026 conversion target has been raised at every single call: low-to-mid 40s in February, mid-40s in April, mid-to-high 40s in July. Net leverage (net debt divided by EBITDA) fell from 0.49x in mid-2025 to 0.42x at year-end to **0.34x at 30 June 2026**. Capital spending is running at 3.8% of revenue. Dividends were raised 10% in early 2026, and more than $370 million has been returned to shareholders since the programme began.

**Growth drivers introduced along the way:** managed pressure drilling, or MPD (a technique for drilling with precise control of downhole pressure, used heavily offshore) has been promoted from a product line to the centrepiece — management sees roughly 30 drillships still to be equipped and claims a strong share of that market. Alongside it: intelligent completions, digital/production optimisation, a Delaware redomestication worth $20–30 million a year in cash tax and administrative savings from 2027, and the acquisition of NCS Multistage, closed 1 September 2026.

**Quietly dropped or demoted:** the 2025 "25 to 75 basis points of annual margin improvement in a flat market" formula still gets cited, but the market has not been flat and the formula has not been testable. Saudi Arabia, talked up through 2025 as the next growth engine, has become a place where a lump-sum turnkey (LSTK) contract was allowed to lapse on price. Venezuela, a genuine new entrant to the story in February 2026, has been consistently framed as 2027-and-beyond optionality rather than a number.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management claim | Where said | What the numbers show | Verdict |

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Stable — with a distinct and deliberate narrowing of what management will promise.**

- **Q1 2025 (defensive, candid):** *"it is very difficult to quantify right now because we don't know exactly what it's going to look like"* on tariffs; *"I sincerely hope I am completely wrong on this."* Management moved from offence to defence before the sector did, and said so.
- **Q2 2025 (defensive, resigned):** *"we anticipate market headwinds will persist for at least another 12 months."*
- **Q3 2025 (turning):** *"I have never been more excited about the future of Weatherford... I think we're really firing on all cylinders"* — but immediately preceded by *"the market is soft."*
- **Q4 2025 (most confident of the six):** a 10% dividend increase, Venezuela introduced as upside, *"we remain optimistic about a stronger 2027."*
- **Q1 2026 (shocked, still specific):** the Iran conflict quantified at *"$30 million to $50 million profit impact over the first half."* Giving a number into an unquantifiable event is a confidence signal in itself.
- **Q2 2026 (chastened but precise):** *"we don't see it increasing right now, and I think that's positive... I do believe it's moderating, but that's always subject to what happens tomorrow"* — and then, ten days later in the same answer, *"a very unfortunate flare-up once again."* On 2027: *"I am not going to give an outlook and guidance for 2027 right now, but... 2027 should definitely be a year of growth."*

The unmistakable shift across the six calls is **from geography-and-product-line granularity to enterprise-level margin and cash metrics**. In April 2025 the company explicitly said its outlook would be *"less granular between geo markets and product lines."* It has never gone back. That is defensible in a market this unstable, but it also means the investor has fewer checkable forecasts than they had two years ago.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: High on what they guide; the earnings-per-share line is not what they guide.**

| Guidance given | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Apr 2025: North America down high-single to mid-double digits, international down low-to-mid-double digits, low-20s EBITDA margin | 2025 revenue −10.8%, margin ~21.7%. **Hit.** |
| Apr 2025: Mexico down ~60% | Full-year Mexico down "a little over 50%". **Close, slightly conservative.** |
| Feb 2025→2026: free cash flow conversion up 100–200 basis points | Delivered +576 basis points. **Materially beat.** |
| Oct 2025: first half 2026 down year on year, second half improvement | First half 2026 revenue $2.257B vs $2.397B — down 5.8%. **Hit on the down leg**; the up leg is not yet proven. |
| Apr 2026: Iran conflict $30–50M first-half profit impact | July 2026: *"within the $30 million-$50 million profit range we outlined."* **Hit.** |
| Jul 2026: Q3 margins up at least 100 basis points; full-year EBITDA $951M–$1,046M; conversion mid-to-high 40s | Reports around 21 October 2026. **Open.** |

**Sandbagging pattern:** yes, and it is systematic — but only on cash. The free-cash-flow conversion target has been raised at four consecutive calls. On revenue there is no sandbagging; there is a consistent, honest tendency to call the downturn early and the recovery too soon.

**Credibility score: 4 of 5.** Management told the market the cycle was turning down before its peers did, quantified an unquantifiable war impact and landed inside its own range, and has beaten every cash target it set. It loses the fifth point for the serially-postponed recovery and for an earnings line that has surprised badly to the downside twice.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

- **Mexico receivables (Podhaizer, Modak, multiple quarters).** For four quarters running analysts have asked whether the state oil company will actually pay. Management's answers have improved from *"we do not have precise visibility"* (Q2 2025) to *"the third straight quarter where we did receive sizable collections"* (Q2 2026). This one has gone the right way, but it remains a single-customer concentration inside the largest swing factor in the cash guide.
- **2027 quantification (West, Q2 2026).** Asked directly to frame 2027, management gave direction without magnitude: *"2027 should definitely be a year of growth... in the next few months, we will be able to calibrate very specifically how much."* That is the pivotal number for the equity, and it will not exist until the February 2027 call.
- **Tariff quantification (Podhaizer, Q1 2025).** Deflected at the time — *"way too difficult and probably too early"* — and it later turned into confirmed margin dilution through the second half of 2025 and specific US product-line damage. The deflection was honest but the outcome was negative.
- **Russia.** Analysts do not ask, and management raised it themselves in Q2 2026 only to note that *"Russia revenues as a percent of enterprise revenue increased"* — mechanically, because everything else shrank. Nobody has pressed on what a sanctions escalation or forced exit would cost. **This is the most significant unasked question on the call.**
- **Pricing.** Rising pricing pressure has been acknowledged in every call since Q2 2025 and never quantified. The Saudi lump-sum contract was allowed to lapse because *"the market is going to be what the market is"* — a polite way of saying a competitor bid below Weatherford's return threshold.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**🔴 Red flags**
- **The recovery has been rescheduled six times** (Q1 2025 → Q2 2025 → Q3 2025 → Q4 2025 → Q1 2026 → Q2 2026). Direction has been right; timing has never been.
- **Q2 2026 earnings of $0.55 against roughly $0.92 expected**, and a 44% effective tax rate against a tax benefit the quarter before. The tax line is volatile enough to make reported earnings a poor guide to the business.
- **Revenue has declined two years running** and 2026 guidance implies a third year below the 2024 peak. EBITDA is guided *below* 2025.
- **Insider behaviour is negative.** On open-market transactions only: 2 purchases totalling 12,000 shares against 12 sales totalling 178,370 shares. The screener's flattering "insider buy ratio" is inflated by share grants and should be ignored.
- **Concentration risk on three axes at once:** one Mexican customer dominating cash-flow variability, a Middle East region that is both the growth engine and the war zone, and a Russian revenue line that is quietly rising as a share of the total.
- **The Saudi lump-sum contract lapse and the Oman contract completion** are real second-half revenue that is gone, replaced by a smaller Marmul extension.

**🟢 Green flags**
- **Net leverage of 0.34x with $1.7B of liquidity** at what management describes as investment-grade-equivalent ratios. For a company that emerged from bankruptcy in 2019, this is the transformation.
- **Free cash flow conversion raised at four consecutive calls**, from low-40s to mid-to-high-40s, against a 50% through-cycle target the chief financial officer has said he privately considers a floor.
- **Margins essentially held** (20.2% in both 2026 quarters) through a war, a Norwegian labour strike, tariff pass-through dilution and pricing pressure — on a revenue base down 15% from peak. Over 2,000 positions and more than $150 million of annualised cost were taken out early.
- **Capital discipline is real, not rhetorical:** capital spending at 3.8% of revenue, two Argentine businesses divested because they were capital-hungry, a Saudi contract walked away from on price.
- **Genuine technology differentiation** in managed pressure drilling, with a deepwater award list in Q2 2026 (Constellation, Ventura, Valaris, Noble, Esso Nigeria, Chevron Australia) that is the strongest in the six-quarter window.
- **Two corporate actions completed in the last three weeks:** the NCS Multistage acquisition closed 1 September 2026, and shareholders approved the Delaware redomestication on 3 September 2026 after the Texas version had failed the 75% Irish threshold in June.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

- **The word "hopeful" is doing enormous work.** It appears in every call from Q1 2025 onward, attached to Saudi recovery, Mexican payments, milder-than-past-cycles discipline and the conflict moderating. When a chief executive's forward statements cluster around hope rather than backlog, the forecast is an expectation, not a commitment.
- **A deliberate vocabulary shift from "revenue" to "quality of revenue."** Q2 2026: *"we will not chase revenue at the expense of returns, and we would rather step away from lower margin work."* That is either genuine discipline or pre-emptive framing for further top-line decline. The Saudi walk-away and the Argentine divestitures suggest it is mostly the former.
- **The chief financial officer transition matters.** Anuj Dhruv arrived in April 2025 on "day three" with no priorities to offer, and within four quarters had refinanced $1.2B of 2030 notes out to 2033, cut roughly $35 million of run-rate interest, driven working capital efficiency from 26.7% to 27% of revenue and back down two consecutive quarters, and pushed the redomestication. The new voice talks in cash metrics and structural cost where the prior narrative talked in geographies.
- **"Capital light" is now the organising principle.** Completions became the largest product line precisely because it is capital-light; the NCS acquisition is justified as *"at its core, a distribution play"* on a *"differentiated capital-light business"*; the digital push is sold on inventory reduction. This is a business consciously re-engineering itself toward lower capital intensity — which is exactly what raises a cyclical's through-cycle free cash flow.
- **An enterprise resource planning replacement running to 2027–2028** is a multi-year execution risk nobody on the calls has stress-tested. Large system replacements at global service companies are a classic source of unplanned working-capital and billing disruption.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Classification: STABLE.** Not strengthening — revenue and EBITDA have fallen two years running and 2026 is guided below 2025. Not deteriorating — free cash flow, conversion, leverage, capital intensity and shareholder returns have all improved every single quarter through the worst of it. What is happening is a cyclical earnings base eroding while the financial quality of the business rises underneath it.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** *the entire upside case is a timing bet on a recovery that this same management team has now rescheduled six consecutive times, and the recovery's driver — global oil-directed capital spending — is one shared macro factor that the investor cannot diversify away inside this position.* The balance sheet means you will not be wiped out waiting. The question is only whether you are being paid to wait, and at roughly 7.6x enterprise value to trailing EBITDA against Halliburton's 8.1x, the answer is that you are being paid very little relative to the nearest true peer.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and stable rather than eroding.** The moat type is **intangible-technology plus switching costs**: managed pressure drilling holds a genuine leadership position in deepwater with an installed rental fleet and aftermarket service agreements attached, and artificial lift rests on a large installed base with real switching friction. The evidence supports narrow, not wide — return on invested capital of about 13.6% on a trailing basis is respectable and has edged *up* (13.1% in the annual figures), and EBITDA margins have been held near 20–22% through a 15% revenue decline, which is not the signature of an eroding franchise. But three larger competitors hold scale advantages, pricing pressure is acknowledged in every recent call, and the company walked away from a Saudi contract because a rival bid below its return threshold. Gross margin is contracting even as EBITDA margin holds, which says cost discipline is offsetting price erosion rather than pricing power defeating it.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** The structural force with a claim on this company's terminal value is the energy transition — a long-run plateau and eventual decline in oil-directed capital spending. Three things keep it at manageable rather than material today: Weatherford's portfolio is weighted toward production optimisation, artificial lift, intervention and mature-field rejuvenation, which are the parts of the spend curve that *rise* as fields age and decline rates bite; energy security has visibly moved from rhetoric into national oil company capital plans; and Brent crude is near $100 a barrel. The cheapness here is therefore **not** a structurally shrinking base — it is a cyclical trough compounded by a regional war. Equally, it is not a fear-print mispricing either, because at roughly a 4% discount to a defensible sum-of-the-parts value there is barely a discount to mis-price.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

bull_thesis:
Weatherford is a post-bankruptcy oilfield-services business that has quietly turned itself into one of the best cash converters in its industry, and it is priced as though it were still the weakest of the four majors. The bull case rests on three legs that are already visible in the numbers, plus one that is not.

The first leg is cash. Free cash flow - the money left after running and re-equipping the business - was $466 million in 2025 at a 43.7% conversion of adjusted operating cash profit, an improvement of 576 basis points on 2024 against management's own promise of 100 to 200 points. In the first half of 2026 conversion ran near 49%, and the second quarter alone delivered $139 million at 62.3% conversion in a quarter disrupted by war, a Norwegian labour strike and deferred Mexican wells. Management has raised its full-year conversion target at four consecutive calls, from the low-40s in February to mid-to-high-40s in July, and the finance chief has said publicly that his private target sits above the stated 50% through-cycle goal. On a trailing twelve-month basis the company produced $525 million of free cash flow against a market value near $6.1 billion - a cash yield close to 8.6%, versus 6.2% at Halliburton, 5.9% at SLB and 5.5% at Baker Hughes. That is the cleanest single argument for owning this: it is the cheapest large oilfield-services name in the world on the metric that actually pays shareholders.

The second leg is the balance sheet, which is no longer a risk factor. Cash of $1.14 billion against $1.62 billion of total debt (including $176 million of leases) leaves net debt of $485 million and a net leverage ratio of 0.34 times - a level management describes as investment-grade equivalent. Total liquidity is $1.7 billion. The 2030 notes were refinanced out to 2033 in September 2025 at what management called the tightest spread to Treasuries an oilfield-services high-yield issuer had achieved, cutting roughly $35 million of annual interest. There is no maturity wall, no covenant pressure and no financing event that can force a bad decision. A cyclical with no solvency risk can wait out a cycle; that is what makes patience investable here rather than merely hopeful.

The third leg is cost and capital discipline that has been proven under fire. More than 2,000 positions and over $150 million of annualised cost came out in 2025, early and ahead of peers. Capital spending runs at 3.8% of revenue. Two Argentine businesses were sold because they were about to become capital-hungry. A Saudi lump-sum turnkey contract was allowed to lapse rather than be renewed at unacceptable pricing. The result is that adjusted operating margins held at roughly 20 to 22% through a 15% revenue decline from the 2024 peak - and the third quarter is guided up at least 100 basis points despite the Middle East conflict and the loss of that Saudi contract. Holding margin flat on a shrinking base is the single hardest thing to do in this industry, and this team has done it for eight quarters.

The fourth leg - the one not yet in the numbers - is the recovery. National oil companies are anchoring capital plans in security of supply; Brent crude sits near $100 a barrel; the deepwater cycle is visibly building, with second-quarter managed-pressure-drilling awards from Constellation, Ventura, Valaris, Noble and Esso Nigeria plus a five-year Chevron framework contract in Australia. Managed pressure drilling - drilling with precise control of downhole pressure - is Weatherford's genuine technology edge, and management sees roughly 30 drillships still to be equipped with it. Add Venezuela, a market that was once $500 million of annual revenue for this company and where management says it has been pleasantly surprised by the pace of reopening, with a tangible 2027 contribution expected. Add the Delaware redomestication approved on 3 September, worth $20-30 million of cash savings a year from 2027. Add NCS Multistage, closed 1 September, a capital-light completions business with at least $15 million of identified cost synergies within eighteen months and a global distribution network to scale into.

For this to work, three conditions must hold: the Middle East conflict must stop deteriorating so that the deferred activity actually returns; Mexican payments must keep arriving at the pace of the last three quarters; and 2027 must deliver the growth management says is coming. If all three hold, 2027 adjusted operating cash profit of $1.1 billion at better than 50% conversion plus the tax savings produces roughly $575 million of free cash flow, and a business converting cash at that rate with 0.3 times leverage does not stay at a 6.5 times multiple.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that Weatherford is a bad company. It is that you are being asked to pay roughly fair value for a business whose revenue has fallen for two straight years, whose recovery has been rescheduled six consecutive times, and whose upside depends entirely on one macro variable you cannot hedge inside the position.

Start with the trajectory. Revenue: $5.51 billion in 2024, $4.92 billion in 2025, a guided $4.54-4.80 billion in 2026. Adjusted operating cash profit is guided at $951 million to $1,046 million this year against roughly $1,066 million last year - so the 2026 guide is a third consecutive year of decline, not a trough with an upturn attached. Reported earnings per share went $6.75 (2024) to $5.93 (2025) to $5.07 on a trailing basis, and the second quarter of 2026 printed $0.55 against roughly $0.92 expected. Each individual decline has an explanation - Mexico, tariffs, the Iran conflict, a Norwegian strike, a 44% effective tax rate - and that is precisely the problem: for eight quarters there has always been an explanation.

Second, the recovery is a promise with a poor track record. In April 2025 the chief executive said headwinds would pass; in July 2025 he said they would persist for at least another twelve months; in October 2025 the hope moved to the second half of 2026; in February 2026 it became a tale of two halves; in April 2026 a new conflict arrived; in July 2026 it required, in his words, a recalibration on timing and pace. Management's own language is still hopeful rather than contracted - on Saudi recovery, on Mexican payments, on the conflict moderating, on industry pricing discipline. On 2027 the chief executive would say only that it should definitely be a year of growth while explicitly declining to size it. The number that matters does not exist until the February 2027 call.

Third, the conflict is not behind them. Management quantified the first-half profit impact at $30-50 million, then said on the July call that they expect it to increase over the year, and described a very unfortunate flare-up once again in the prior ten to twelve days, with continuing disruption in Bahrain, Qatar, Iraq and Kuwait. The cruel irony is structural: the $100 Brent price that is supposed to drive the recovery is itself partly a product of the same regional conflict that is suppressing Weatherford's activity in that region. High oil from a supply shock in the geography where you operate is a headwind, not a tailwind.

Fourth, the second half has identified revenue losses that are certain: the Saudi lump-sum contract concluded, and management said this will be further visible in the second half; the Oman integrated contract completed; and the replacement Marmul extension is smaller. Pricing pressure has been acknowledged on every call since mid-2025 and never quantified.

Fifth, concentration on three axes. One Mexican customer remains, by management's own words, the biggest driver of variability in the cash guidance - and the cash guidance is the entire bull case. The Middle East is simultaneously the growth engine and the war zone. And Russian revenue as a share of the enterprise has been rising, which management attributes to everything else shrinking - a sanctions escalation or forced exit is an unhedged tail that no analyst on any of the six calls has pressed.

Sixth, the people who know most are selling. On open-market transactions only, insiders bought 12,000 shares across two purchases and sold 178,370 shares across twelve. The flattering buy ratio in the screening data is inflated by share grants and should be disregarded.

Seventh, and decisively, the valuation is not distressed. At roughly 7.6 times enterprise value to trailing operating cash profit, Weatherford trades at only about a 7% discount to Halliburton's 8.1 times - and Halliburton is the correct comparison, because the 12 times multiples at SLB and Baker Hughes are inflated by large non-oilfield digital and industrial-technology businesses. The deep-value label in the screen comes from book-value and peak-earnings models: a stated 79% margin of safety and a $147.54 fair value both anchor on a 2024 earnings peak that will not be repeated soon, and one of the five internal models already reads fair to negative. Strip the peak-earnings artifact and the margin of safety is a few percent, not seventy.

What confirms the bear: a third-quarter print around 21 October that misses the $235-265 million operating-cash-profit guide or fails to deliver the promised 100 basis points of margin expansion; any Mexican payment interruption; a further Middle East escalation; or a 2027 guide in February that comes in flat rather than growing. There is no solvency risk here - just the risk of owning a fairly-priced cyclical for two years while the recovery is rescheduled a seventh time.
consensus_delta:
For a business the screen labels deeply undervalued, the right question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a company with stable earnings power. Our answer is that it is not - and that the apparent bargain is largely an artifact of how the value was measured.

Where the screen is wrong. The stated 79% margin of safety and the $147.54 fair value are anchored on 2024, which was the peak: revenue $5.51 billion, earnings per share $6.75. Applying peak multiples to a company guiding 2026 revenue of $4.54-4.80 billion and operating cash profit below 2025's level produces a number with no claim on reality. The internal models already disagree with each other by an enormous margin - a Graham-style reading says 71% undervalued while one of the other five reads negative - and wide model dispersion on a cyclical is nearly always a peak-earnings artifact rather than a hidden bargain. The screen's book-value-per-share growth of 36% a year over five years is likewise a post-bankruptcy accounting recovery, not compounding.

Where the street is wrong, and it cuts both ways. The consensus target of $135 is not a street-wide view: only one price target was published in the last quarter, five in the last year averaging $102.80, and the newest is 55 days old. The two recent marks bracket the argument - UBS upgraded to buy on 29 July with a $114 target when the stock was $83.58; Barclays carried $156 on 17 June at $97.85. Neither number has been refreshed for the September rate shock. A $135 consensus implies roughly 9.5 times enterprise value to operating cash profit, which is above Halliburton today, for a business with less scale and more geographic concentration. That target is stale, thin and too high.

Where we genuinely disagree with the market - and it is a smaller gap than it looks. The market prices Weatherford's cash conversion as though it were a cyclical accident. It is not: conversion has been raised at four consecutive calls, capital spending is structurally lower at 3.8% of revenue, working capital efficiency has improved two quarters running, the Delaware move adds $20-30 million of annual cash savings from 2027, and the refinancing cut roughly $35 million of interest. That is a durable step-change in free cash flow per dollar of revenue, and on free cash flow yield this is the cheapest large oilfield-services name in the world at 8.6% against Halliburton's 6.2%. But the market has already awarded most of that: closing even half the gap to Halliburton gets you to about $86, and the stock is $84.89. The disagreement is worth a few percent, not a re-rating.

The one genuinely underappreciated point is the earnings-per-share optics. Reported earnings fell 71% year on year in the second quarter, and the headline reads like a collapse. It is not: adjusted operating cash profit fell about 12%, and the gap is a $33 million tax charge on $75 million of pre-tax income - a 44% effective rate - against a tax benefit the prior quarter. This company misses consensus earnings estimates (four beats in seven quarters) because the tax and below-the-line lines are volatile, while it consistently hits the operating and cash figures it actually guides. Anyone screening on earnings-per-share momentum is reading the wrong line. That argues the business is better than the print - not that the stock is cheap.

The hardest-edged date on the calendar and the first real test of the second-half recovery promise: $1.105-1.155 billion of revenue, $235-265 million of adjusted operating cash profit, margins up at least 100 basis points, more than $100 million of free cash flow, all while absorbing the concluded Saudi lump-sum contract, the completed Oman contract and the Norwegian strike. What would make this actionable today is a price, not an event: the case becomes live in the $70-75 range, where the adverse scenario is largely in the price and the cash yield approaches 10%. That is the specific level we are waiting for.

The chief executive was explicit that the impact will unlikely go to zero until there is a firm and permanent resolution. The bar management set is specific: $1.105-1.155 billion of revenue, $235-265 million of adjusted operating cash profit, margins up at least 100 basis points, and more than $100 million of free cash flow. The business case is not in dispute. The problem remains the price, and it has barely moved in our favour despite an 11.5% fall. That is the counterintuitive heart of this. The shares dropped from $95.88 on 4 September to $84.89 today - but roughly two-thirds of that is the oil-services complex de-rating 7.4% over the same window, and the reason it de-rated is that the discount rate moved: the Federal Reserve raised rates on 16 September for the first time since July 2023, sixteen of eighteen participants pencil another increase this year, and the ten-year Treasury closed at or above 5% for the first time since 2007. When the risk-free rate is 5%, a cyclical with a back-loaded recovery is worth less, and our own fair value fell roughly in step with the share price. Our base case is $88 against a $84.89 price - a margin of safety of a few percent, nowhere near the 20-30% this book requires before committing capital.

The market environment makes it worse, not better, in two specific ways. First, independence of drivers: the entire upside rests on global oil-directed capital spending, a single shared macro factor, in a market where that is exactly the concentration to avoid. Second, and more subtly, the $100 Brent price that is supposed to signal the recovery is partly a product of the same Middle East conflict that is suppressing Weatherford's activity in the Middle East. High oil from a supply shock in the geography where you operate is a headwind wearing a tailwind's clothes. What this thesis does not do is depend on rate cuts, which is to its credit.

On the catalyst we apply this book's neutrality rule strictly. Two dated events completed and are spent: the NCS Multistage acquisition closed 1 September, and shareholders approved the Delaware move on 3 September. Neither is penalised and neither is rewarded; both are simply credited in the base case, and together they are worth a few dollars a share. The forward driver - the second-half-2026-into-2027 recovery - is a soft catalyst with no fixed date, and it has now been rescheduled six consecutive quarters. We do not mark the name down for that; we mark it down for the absence of a discount.

The deep-value label does not survive contact with the live numbers. The 79% margin of safety and the $147.54 fair value are anchored on 2024 peak earnings that 2026 guidance will not come near; the internal models disagree violently, which on a cyclical is the signature of a peak-earnings artifact. Priced honestly against the only true peer - Halliburton, since SLB's and Baker Hughes's 12 times multiples are inflated by large non-oilfield businesses - Weatherford trades at 7.6 times operating cash profit against 8.1 times: a 7% discount. The one real relative-value argument is cash conversion, an 8.6% free cash flow yield against Halliburton's 6.2%, and closing even half that gap is worth about $86 a share. The market has already paid for most of it.

What we are waiting for, specifically: the case becomes live around $70-75, where the adverse scenario is largely in the price and the cash yield approaches 10%. Below $67 - our adverse case, which already assumes a persisting conflict and operating cash profit falling to $900 million - this would be a clear commitment, because the balance sheet means the downside is a long flat period rather than a permanent loss of capital. The other route in is evidence rather than price: a third-quarter print around 21 October that clears the margin promise, followed by a February 2027 guide with revenue back above $5 billion. That would convert a hope into a number, and we would revisit immediately.

Until one of those arrives, this is a good company at a fair price in a market that is repricing every fair-priced cyclical downward. Fair is not enough. Pass, and keep it close.
